# This startup wants to build an army of humanoid robot soldiers

By[Lloyd Lee](https://www.businessinsider.com/author/lloyd-lee)

You're currently following this author!

![Phantom robot](https://i.insider.com/69ebc27ba98bc8fdc096e972?width=700)

Phantom, a humanoid robot built by Foundation, was sent to Ukraine for a pilot demonstration of a supply pickup scenario.Courtesy Foundation

Apr 26, 2026, 4:11 AM ET

- Foundation is a startup building general-purpose humanoid robots.
- Two of Foundation's robots were sent to Ukraine for a demo of a supply transport scenario.
- CEO Sankaet Pathak said he sees humanoids becoming valuable for precision operations in warfare.

[Humanoid robots](https://www.businessinsider.com/humanoid-robot-companies-us-tesla-figure-1x-agility-apptronik-2025-11) rather than flesh-and-blood soldiers could one day take on some of the most dangerous jobs in war — and one startup is already testing that idea in Ukraine.

Loading audio narration...

Sankaet Pathak, cofounder and CEO of Foundation, said there's a "moral imperative" to put humanoid robots on the front lines rather than in [people's kitchens](https://www.businessinsider.com/sunday-robotics-home-robot-training-hands-loading-dishwasher-2025-11).

"I thought all of this stuff around home use was kind of stupid," Pathak told Business Insider. "I feel like people can make the coffee and fold their laundry. I was like, 'We need to do something else.'"

Advancements in [drone technology](https://www.businessinsider.com/iran-war-us-top-allies-fall-behind-in-drone-defense-2026-3) and robotics are now central to the arsenal of modern warfare, enabling precision attacks at scale and at lower cost; however, that capability hasn't always translated into clean, risk-free operations.

In the age of smart weapons and AI-enabled, autonomous systems, modern warfare still carries a high risk of [civilian casualties](https://www.businessinsider.com/us-drone-strike-kills-10-afghan-civilians-not-isolated-incident-2021-8), especially in dense [urban environments](https://www.businessinsider.com/israel-gaza-urban-warfare-tactics-lessons-nato-2024-8).

![A robot packs boxes](data:image/svg+xml,%3C%3Fxml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'%3F%3E%3Csvg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='1' height='1'/%3E)

Foundation wants to deploy its robots for reconnaissance and supply logistics.



Foundation



Pathak said the current approach to war is often "brute force," either risking soldiers' lives or destroying a building to eliminate a single target.

He believes that in the future, humanoids could execute "surgical" operations, such as extracting a target. Near-term, they could support military operations such as reconnaissance and logistics.

Foundation said it recently conducted a test that could pave the way for those missions.

In February, the startup sent two of its Phantom robots to an undisclosed location in Ukraine for a closed pilot demonstration.

"You can hear bombs go off. You can hear electricity get cut. You're actively in a warzone," Pathak said of Foundation's visit to the country, which for years has been fighting off a Russian invasion. "Most of the places are a battlefield as soon as you start going out of Kyiv."

The CEO said the Phantom test solely focused on "supply pickup" to demonstrate that bipedal robots can effectively "carry supplies from outside to inside and avoid a soldier getting shot at."

There was "significant interest based on what has been communicated" to the company, Pathak said. A spokesperson for Foundation said the startup has also secured a $24 million contract with the Pentagon. Eric Trump, the president's son, was appointed chief strategy advisor in March.

## Humanoid troops aren't ready for deployment

Pathak said he didn't want to "overstate" the Ukraine pilot. A large gap still exists between a humanoid that can slowly clean a test kitchen and one that can usean M4 carbine in a battlefield firefight.

Battery life and durability are among the constraints. Pathak said robot soldiers need longer battery life and must withstand water, dust, and shock.

![Phantom, humanoid robot.](data:image/svg+xml,%3C%3Fxml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'%3F%3E%3Csvg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='1' height='1'/%3E)

Pathak said the test demonstrated that bipedal robots can be used for certain applications.



Courtesy Foundation



Reliable manipulation — the ability for a robot to pick up an item and do something with it, like pulling the trigger on a rifle — also remains a major technological bottleneck.

"Right now, the big engineering hurdle is how do you build a highly-dextrous hand that is reliable, easier to manufacture, isn't too massive, and isn't too expensive," Pathak said.

The CEO offered ambitious predictions for overcoming these challenges, saying that key engineering hurdles could be solved within a few years and that humanoid robots could carry out complex missions, such as target extraction, within five to 10 years.

Beyond the technical questions, ethical dilemmas surrounding [autonomous weaponry](https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-claude-ai-military-use-dario-amodei-2026-2), including concerns of accountability when humans are no longer in the loop, are also a consideration.

Pathak said that while there isn't a simple line that can be drawn around autonomy, in ordinary circumstances, "you probably want a human in the loop before any kind of kill action is invoked." Many Western militaries have made that a priority amid rapid technological advances in artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, though the extent remains an active debate.

"So if you actually need to shoot a gun, you need a human to really sign off, which is what happens with drones today as well," he said. "But then there are exceptions to those cases as well, like an anti-drone gun or the [Iron Dome](https://www.businessinsider.com/israel-iron-dome-missile-defense-system-history-2024-9). Those, you cannot wait for human reaction times because the alternative is 100% certainty of fatality."

The defense industry at large pushes robotics and autonomous weapons as a matter of national security. Anduril cofounder Palmer Luckey has repeatedly said that the United States needs to be ahead of China on [AI weapons](https://www.businessinsider.com/palmer-luckey-ai-weapons-pandoras-box-china-arms-race-2025-4). The top US admiral in the Pacific said this week that America's AI technology lead over China is only six months to a year at best.

Unlike many other companies, Foundation has been particularly outspoken on using humanoids on the battlefield.

"Courage comes in limited supply," Pathak said, while arguing that China is not having the same debate over military humanoids and that the US, Europe, and their allies need to be on alert. "If you build a utopia," he said, "you have to be able to defend it."

Quick SummaryHide

According to Business Insider, startup **Foundation** sent two humanoid robots, including a unit called **Phantom**, to Ukraine for a pilot demonstration of a supply pickup and transport scenario. Business Insider reports CEO Sankaet Pathak described a "moral imperative" to deploy humanoid robots in frontline roles and said that within **5 to 10 years** such robots could be capable of extracting targets, per the article. The demonstration and CEO comments underscore ongoing private-sector experimentation with humanoid systems for precision operations in conflict zones, a development that raises operational, ethical, and regulatory questions for engineers and policymakers, Business Insider reports.

### What happened

According to Business Insider, startup **Foundation** sent two humanoid robots, including a unit identified as **Phantom**, to Ukraine for a pilot demonstration of a supply pickup and transport scenario. Business Insider reports CEO **Sankaet Pathak** said there is a "moral imperative" to put humanoid robots into frontline roles and that, in his view, humanoids could be able to extract targets within **5 to 10 years**.

### Technical details

Industry reporting indicates the exercise focused on logistics support rather than lethal engagement; Business Insider frames the Ukraine demo as a supply-transfer scenario using Foundation's humanoid hardware. Business Insider does not provide published specifications, autonomy stack details, or sensor/actuator descriptions for the robots in the field. Foundation has not released a technical white paper in the Business Insider article excerpt.

### Industry context

Editorial analysis: Companies testing humanoid platforms in operational settings are accelerating the transition from lab validation to field trials. Observed patterns in similar deployments show teams often iterate rapidly on perception, control, and human-robot interfaces after early demos, and noncombat logistics missions are a common early use case before more complex tasks are attempted.

### Context and significance

Editorial analysis: Private-sector demonstrations in active conflict zones amplify ethical and regulatory scrutiny because they expose gaps in doctrine, verification, and safety guarantees. For practitioners, the combination of hardware ruggedization, low-latency communications, and reliable autonomy is technically demanding; professional teams deploying such systems typically face integration and verification workstreams that are orders of magnitude larger than bench evaluations.

### What to watch

For practitioners: follow technical disclosures from Foundation and independent verification from third parties about autonomy levels, rules of engagement encoding, and fail-safe behaviors. For policymakers and ethicists: watch for statements from defense authorities and international organizations about permissible roles, export controls, and testing restrictions. Business Insider does not quote government or independent evaluators in the article excerpt, and Foundation has not issued a separate public technical dossier in that reporting.

## Scoring Rationale

Field testing of humanoid robots in an active conflict zone is a notable step for robotics and autonomy, with practical implications for hardware, autonomy stacks, and policy. The story is important to practitioners but is an early-stage demonstration rather than a production deployment.

# ‘Robots don’t bleed’: Ukraine to replace frontline troops with 25,000 ground robots

[![fot. TVP](https://s2.tvp.pl/images2/2/d/f/uid_2df9dd46bb37407fbfce110311856f7c_width_50_play_0_pos_0_gs_0_height_50.png)\\
Ewan Jones](https://tvpworld.com/82040614/ewan-jones)

Edited by: Ed Wight

20.04.2026, 12:53


![Unmanned ground systems are increasingly being used for combat operations. (PAP/Ukrinform/Oleksandr Klymenko)](https://s6.tvp.pl/images2/6/a/d/uid_6ad19b9983e543a0859faf1eab0d8ec3_width_1200_play_0_pos_0_gs_0_height_675.jpg)Unmanned ground systems are increasingly being used for combat operations. (PAP/Ukrinform/Oleksandr Klymenko)

Ukraine is planning to replace frontline troops with 25,000 unmanned ground robots in the first half of this year, the country’s defense minister has said.

Ukraine has already signed contracts to the value of UAH 11 billion (€210 million) for unmanned ground systems as the devices carry out ever more functions, including combat missions.

“Our goal— 100% of frontline logistics should be performed by robotic systems,” Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on April 18, announcing the plans for 25,000 more units.

The new procurement target—double the figure for the whole of 2025—aims to capitalize on Ukraine’s growing battlefield advantge in unmanned systems.

Analysts say the embattled country is way ahead of the curve as it seeks to counter its numerical disadvantage against Russia as well as to use its expertise to forge strategic alliances with other countries—and secure sales.

![Ukraine wants all frontline logitics to be performer by machine. Photo: PAP/Ukrinform/Tarasov  ](https://s10.tvp.pl/images2/0/d/7/uid_0d75d1439aad4c849102ba844c3bc2f2_width_1025_play_0_pos_0_gs_0_height_0.jpg)Ukraine wants all frontline logitics to be performer by machine. Photo: PAP/Ukrinform/Tarasov

## **The future is now**

Ukraine’s experience in unmanned aerial systems is well documented, but behind the headlines there have been quieter advances in both sea and land platforms.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has touted the fact that autonomous systems recently [took a manned Russian position](https://tvpworld.com/92658797/kyiv-says-it-took-russian-position-using-only-robots), forcing the soldiers to surrender.

In a world first in April, [Ukraine made military history](https://tvpworld.com/92788822/ukraine-sea-drone-launched-uav-intercepts-russian-shahed) with the first case of an enemy attack drone being brought down by an interceptor drone launched from an autonomous naval platform, or sea drone.

The previous month, a San Francisco-based tech company sent two humanoid robot soldiers to the Ukrainian front line as part of field tests.

![ US-based firm Foundation has sent two humanoid robots to Ukraine for testing. Photo: Foundation](https://s7.tvp.pl/images2/7/3/b/uid_73bd64d23ac64a3aa0da70d14978f451_width_1025_play_0_pos_0_gs_0_height_0.jpg) US-based firm Foundation has sent two humanoid robots to Ukraine for testing. Photo: Foundation

And the rate of automation is accelerating rapidly.

While a year ago, fully automated operations were an experimental rarity, in the first three months of 2026, robotic systems carried out a total of 22,000 frontline missions.

“In other words, lives were saved more than 22,000 times when a robot went into the most dangerous areas instead of a warrior,” President Zelenskyy said. “This is about high technology protecting the highest value—human life.”

The president’s thoughts were echoed by Mykola 'Makar' Zinkevych, commander of the unit behind the operation that captured the Russian position.

“Human life is precious, but robots don’t bleed,” Zinkevych told US news service CNN, adding that scale is key.

“We must understand that we will never have more personnel, and we will never have a numerical advantage over the enemy,” he said. "So, we need to achieve this advantage through technology.”

![Ukraine has also developed a range of naval drones. Photo: PAP/Ukrinform/Danylo Antoniuk](https://s4.tvp.pl/images2/4/9/9/uid_499adf5a29af40fb968b2f525475fcf9_width_1025_play_0_pos_0_gs_0_height_0.jpg)Ukraine has also developed a range of naval drones. Photo: PAP/Ukrinform/Danylo Antoniuk

## **Scaling is key**

But while Moscow is behind in the race, it is making advances and learning from experience, Zinkevych said.

Ukraine’s defense ministry has implemented measures to maintain momentum and keep Kyiv’s advantage.

Among the plans is a specialized center to coordinate the deployment of ground robotic systems as well as efforts to ramp up related fields, including engineering systems for mining and demining, as well as combat robotic platforms.

“Our focus—low-cost and effective strike ground systems that the state can scale quickly,” Defense Minister Fedorov said.

Zinkevych, a combat veteran who used to be skeptical of battlefield automation, says he has become totally sold on the concept.

"My position is that robotic ground systems need to be developed much faster, on a much larger scale, and implemented as a global system for use on the battlefield,” he said.

news.title: Russia triggered robot warfare — and created a monster in Ukraine
news.snippet: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told industry workers, "For the first time in this war's history, an enemy position was taken exclusively by unmanned...
news.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told industry workers, "For the first time in this war's history, an enemy position was taken exclusively by unmanned...
news.markdown:
[![NY Post](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/D21CF7637CF27B5C69ED194FC92011091FC7D873EF5FAA0CFD4499702BC9A1EE/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w194_h40;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fs.yimg.com%2Fos%2Fcreatr-uploaded-images%2F2024-01%2F46c6ce20-b635-11ee-babf-0468df94f866)](https://nypost.com/)

David Hambling

Mon, April 20, 2026 at 10:10 AM UTC

0

![Ground robotic systems and drones used in the Ukraine War](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/62BE980653BF27038346536A92605A4FA34A837B85F69A7CA6FBBCFF838C42C2/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w976_h651;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Faol_ny_post_us_news_articles_123%2F58222a93e76b4f3a948374a37a41df8f)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told industry workers, "For the first time in this war's history, an enemy position was taken exclusively by unmanned platforms and drones."

Vladimir Putin has created a monster — and it may destroy him.

As President Volodymyr Zelensky has made plain, Putin’s war of choice against Ukraine has brought on the age of war robots.

“For the first time in this war’s history, an enemy position was taken exclusively by unmanned platforms and drones,” Zelensky [told defense industry workers](https://www.aol.com/news/ukraine-captures-enemy-russian-position-120100009.html) last week.

“The occupiers surrendered, and this operation was completed without infantry involvement and without losses on our side.”

For the last four years, Russia’s big advantage in this war has been manpower.

It’s been able to flood the zone with troops in numbers Ukraine has struggled to match.

By replacing flesh-and-blood soldiers with mechanical recruits, Kyiv is negating that advantage.

It’s also opening the door to a nightmarish new type of warfare in which machines hunt down and exterminate humans.

Remote-control combat vehicles date back, ironically enough, to the “Teletanks” developed by the Soviet Union in the 1930s.

These were obsolete light tanks armed with flamethrowers to assault defended positions.

But they were difficult to control via unreliable radio connections, and the idea was soon dropped.

By the 1970s, small remote-controlled vehicles found a military niche in bomb disposal, but efforts to add weapons to these robots were unsuccessful.

And while the US deployed armed SWORDS/Talon robots to Iraq in 2007, they were never used in action, apparently due to concerns over reliability and the potential for bad publicity.

The Russians did use Uran-9, a small robotic tank, in Syria, but the results were uneven; it suffered communication problems that left the vehicle stranded, and it has not been seen in Ukraine.

Navigation on the ground is more challenging than flying — which is why [aerial drones are common](https://www.aol.com/news/amazon-customers-furious-delivery-drones-172354350.html) but ground vehicles, from [self-driving cars](https://www.aol.com/news/la-enlists-waymo-fight-potholes-152628447.html) to [sidewalk delivery robots](https://nypost.com/2026/04/10/us-news/philadelphians-attack-uber-eats-delivery-robots-one-month-after-launch/), are still a novelty.

They easily get confused or stuck: In January, a delivery robot got [caught on train tracks in Miami](https://www.aol.com/news/malfunctioned-uber-eats-delivery-robot-223022896.html) and was obliterated by a locomotive.

Ukraine has been tackling the challenge of effective ground robots, or Uncrewed Ground Vehicles, in the same way it evolved drones.

As with drones, the emphasis is on building low-cost systems that leverage commercial technology, getting them out into the field to generate real-world feedback, and iterating rapidly.

Advertisement

The Ukrainians say they can do in weeks what takes years in the West.

Finding a way around obstacles is still a challenge for Ukraine’s UGVs, so the robot operator is teamed with a drone crew with an overhead view to spot the best route.

Robots were initially used for logistics runs, carrying supplies the dangerous last few miles to the front line.

They have since taken on more demanding roles like casualty evacuation and mine-laying — and increasing numbers of videos show armed robots fighting at the front.

DevDroid is a typical example of a Ukrainian combat robot.

About the size of a quad bike, it has a top speed of 4 mph and packs a .50 caliber machine gun with 300 rounds.

Mykola Zinkevych, commander of the 3rd Assault Brigade, says a DevDroid occupied a front line position and fought off Russian troops solo with no soldiers present for 45 days, returning to base at intervals for recharging and reloading.

And, as Zelensky reported, Ukraine is also carrying out robot-only assaults with a mixture of drones and UGVs, using aerial drones to identify threats and point to targets for robot operators.

Such operations currently only involve a handful of machines, but Ukraine plans to produce 20,000 UGVs this year and could scale up rapidly.

In March, Andriy Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, said that in 2026 UGVs would replace 30% of infantry at the front — and that the figure could rise to 80% in the near future.

Military analysts argue that robots can’t truly replace infantry until they can go inside buildings, occupy trenches and perform similar tasks requiring physical flexibility.

That might happen sooner than you think: The Ukrainian military has already experimented with [dog-like quadruped robots](https://www.aol.com/news/meet-100k-robodog-spot-patrols-220143412.html), and recently took delivery of two US-made [Phantom Mk1 humanoid robots](https://nypost.com/2025/02/18/lifestyle/war-robot-designed-for-defense-bizarrely-performs-dj-set-at-nightclub-a-fun-moment/) for testing.

Kyiv has been a reluctant participant in the robot wars.

Its military has turned to technology out of sheer necessity, to reduce the need for soldiers on the front line and to cut casualties.

But Ukraine means to win — and if survival means [sending in Terminator-like machines](https://www.aol.com/news/ukraine-used-record-7k-robot-205334414.html), the nation will not hesitate.

Putin’s invasion [may finally break](https://www.aol.com/news/putin-accidentally-created-high-tech-234540998.html) against a wall of unyielding robot soldiers, operated by crews many miles from the front line.

And that will change war everywhere, forever.

The battlefield of the future with be fully mechanized, and combatants facing each other directly will seem as quaint as fighting with swords.

_David Hambling is the author of “Swarm Troopers: How Small Drones Will Conquer the World.”_
